1:
The inference rests on the whole preceding argument: because Jesus is above prophets and angels, the new revelation is above the old. Calvin states the proportion, that the higher Christ stands above the angels the more reverence the Gospel claims above the Law, and meets the objection that this degrades God, both being his: the fuller he reveals himself, the more our reverence should rise, his greatness not being at all times equally made known. He adds that the Law was Christ's too, though in it he showed himself darkly and as under coverings. Then the verb divides them. Ellicott says the familiar rendering, which came in with the Geneva Bible, gives the sense but inverts the figure: it should be lest we drift away, since it is the man carried off by the current. Robertson agrees, glossing an old verb meaning to flow past, picturing a swimmer swept beyond an anchorage within reach. Clarke, Wesley, Henry and Calvin keep the other figure, a leaking vessel with gaping staves; Calvin defends it from the contrast, to give heed being to hold a thing and its opposite to let it run out as through a sieve.

The second verse argues from the lesser to the greater, and the question is which word is meant. Ellicott renders it through angels, the word being God's while they were the medium, and takes it of the Mosaic law. He admits the Old Testament yields one text only, the coming from Sinai amid myriads of holy ones, where the Greek version adds angels at his right hand; and he shows the belief was current in the apostolic age from Philo, and from a speech of Herod which Josephus records. Gill cites the same speech, adding that the angels formed in the air the voices heard. Barnes is more cautious, calling it the common opinion of the Hebrews; Robertson notes it is not in the Old Testament but in Josephus. Clarke dissents, thinking the writer means not the Law but the particular messages God sent by angels, as to Lot. On steadfast they agree: firm, settled, authoritative; and Calvin takes the clause about punishment as expounding that firmness, a doctrine God avenges being no light matter. Robertson observes that the two nouns for the offence are no mere pairing, one meaning to step aside, the other to neglect to hear, which Wesley renders commission of sin and omission of duty.

On the third verse the weight falls on one word: the charge is neglect, not opposition. Clarke says those meant are not only they who oppose or persecute, but they who pay no regard and never lay it to heart, sinning against the very means of their deliverance, and having refused the one remedy must perish. Calvin says the verb is literally not to care for, and that salvation stands here for the doctrine of it, since God will have men saved no other way; whoever seeks it elsewhere seeks it by another power, which is extreme madness. Barnes turns this into homely cases: a man in business need not commit forgery to ruin himself, only neglect it, and a man drifting above Niagara need not move an oar. Ellicott and Robertson both notice what the verse concedes about its author, ranking himself with those who had not heard the Lord directly but had the word made sure by those who did, and how sharply this differs from the apostle who insisted he had his doctrine from Christ himself. On the fourth verse Calvin and Robertson distinguish the three names for the miracles: a wonder attracts attention, a power shows whose power it is, a sign discloses the purpose; Ellicott takes the compound verb strictly, as bearing witness with the preachers; Wesley separates the signs done while the Lord lived from the distributions given after his exaltation; Gill, that God was testifying to their commission.
5:
The fifth verse resumes the comparison broken off after chapter one. Ellicott ties it both ways, back to the angels called ministering spirits and forward to the salvation just spoken of, and would render it did he subject. On the world to come, Clarke reports the Jewish phrase for the days of the Messiah and prefers it, noting that Macknight took the words of the future glory instead, and of the angel who brought Israel into the land. Wesley agrees, adding that the dispensation was called the world to come though it is still in great measure to come, and that in it the Son alone presides. Ellicott distinguishes the word here, which means the inhabited earth, from another elsewhere translated the same way, and holds that the period meant follows the exaltation, though prophecy blends what we must distinguish. Henry presses the negative until it yields a positive: God would not put so great a trust in his holy ones, his angels being too weak for such a charge. Chrysostom leaves exposition and turns on his hearers, wishing he knew whether any listen with fitting earnestness, and promising to question them privately on what they retain.

The manner of the citation interests them as much as the matter. Ellicott observes that the writer usually quotes Scripture as God's own utterance, and that since this passage addresses God he could not do so here, yet seems glad to avoid naming the prophet; the vagueness is a mannerism common in Philo, as Robertson notes. Clarke and Gill both insist it is not ignorance: Clarke shows the same form in Philo and in Plato citing Heraclitus, and calls it reverence rather than doubt; Gill says the writer knew perfectly well, but wrote to Jews familiar with the text, whose own way of citing was exactly this. On the question itself Robertson notes the interrogative is neuter, not who but what, so that man's insignificance is implied, and that son of man here has no Messianic force but is used as in Ezekiel. Clarke goes behind the Greek to two Hebrew words the English levels: one is the name given at creation, the other signifies sick, weak and wretched, and was never given to man until after his fall. Wesley reads the psalm as composed on a clear moonlit night, the sun being never mentioned among the luminaries, and observes that the sense rises, for we may be mindful of the absent, but to visit denotes the care of a present God.

The clause about the angels is where Hebrew and Greek part company. Ellicott says the Greek represents the Hebrew faithfully at every point but this, where the original has a little less than God, and thinks the translators softened a bold expression about the Deity. Gill defends the apostle's rendering from the Targum and four Jewish commentators; Wesley and Clarke keep the stronger sense, Clarke adding that said of man as he left his Maker's hands it sets him at the head of all God's works. Robertson notes the same word is used of judges elsewhere and is certainly not God in our sense, and that the qualifying phrase is one of degree here but of time in Isaiah, which is how Clarke takes it when applying it to Christ. Calvin faces the harder objection, that the psalm speaks of mankind and not one man, and answers that Adam was given the world and by his defection lost the right to it, God leaving tokens of that loss in the beasts that attack us and the earth that disappoints. On the last clause all agree the dominion is broken. Ellicott keeps the repeated verb audible, Barnes lists tempest and pestilence, and Robertson says not even a century of telescopes, submarines and radio has brought man to that goal. Calvin closes it: what is wanting will in its time be completed.
9:
The verse answers the not yet of the last, and Robertson states the turn plainly: we do not see man triumphant, but we do see Jesus; death has defeated man, and this man has conquered death. Gill adds that the seeing is not with bodily eyes but with the mind. Ellicott would reorder the clauses so the sight comes first, and notes an apparent departure from the psalm, since words that there mark dignity here mark humiliation, though the difference is not essential, the position of man being signified either way. Whether the phrase means a little in degree or in time divides them. Calvin holds for degree, since that is plainly the sense in the psalm, and presses a further point: Christ still continues in the nature he assumed, though it is now refined and perfected, so that the inferiority is no passing episode but is compensated by a superiority of honour. Ellicott and Barnes agree, Barnes taking it of rank on earth. Clarke and Robertson read it of time, for a little while; Wesley leaves the phrase alone and glosses the angels instead, as those who can neither suffer nor die.

On the connection between suffering and crown they are careful. Barnes insists the point is not that he suffered but that on account of it he was crowned: the words mean not that he was made lower in order to die, but that as a reward for having died he was raised. Robertson takes the preposition in the same causal sense and notes the crowning is already done. Ellicott observes what the verse does not say, that we see all things put in subjection to him, which would contradict what comes later; other words of the psalm are substituted that leave the subjection incomplete, the exalting of the one not replacing the exalting of the many but making it possible. He also feels the difficulty of the last clause's position, since it can hardly be said that Jesus was crowned in order to taste death, and relieves it by the consideration that the efficacy of the sufferings depends on their triumphant issue, which a Christian cannot separate from them even in thought. Calvin turns it into a final cause: Christ is crowned that every knee should bow, whence we may reason that all things are delivered into his hand; and he guards against the notion that Christ earned eternal life first for himself and then for us.

The last clause draws out the most. Clarke expounds it by the ancient custom of despatching criminals with a cup of poison, recalling how unjustly Socrates was condemned and how cheerfully he drank it off, and then turns the picture round: the whole race stands condemned, each with his own poisoned cup, and Jesus takes it from every hand and drinks the dregs. He asks whether this is not the Gethsemane cup. On the verb, Ellicott calls tasting death a familiar Hebraism, and Robertson insists it is no rapid sip but a bitter experience, the seeing of death. Calvin says the same more bluntly, that to taste food in Scripture is to eat and to taste death is to die; and while he will neither refute nor condemn the father who made it a touching of the lips because Christ came out a conqueror, he doubts the writer meant anything so fine. He thinks the same father's image of a physician sipping first to encourage the patient falls short, since what is meant is that Christ took on him what was due to us. On the extent, Robertson notes it is every one and not everything, as some early Greek theologians took it; Wesley, every man that ever was or will be born. Both Clarke and Robertson record the rival reading, apart from God for by the grace of God, which Clarke thinks a marginal gloss crept into the text.
10:
The tenth verse answers an objection rather than opening a new theme. Barnes and Clarke both name it: a Jew would urge that the Messiah is never to be conquered or to die but to be victorious for ever, and that a man of sorrows cannot be what is claimed. The answer is that the suffering was fitting, and fitting to God rather than to us. Robertson points out that the impersonal verb means to be seemly, and that the pronoun refers to the Father and not the Son, who is named separately as author. He also finds in the two prepositions a repudiation of the Gnostic scheme, the universe existing for God as its reason and coming to be through him as its agent, with no intermediaries. Ellicott puts it that what seemed to Jews incredible was ordained by grace, and that if the means men wondered at were God's own choice, none may doubt their fitness. Calvin adds a pastoral point: the circumlocution replaces the bare name of God to remind us that what he appoints is best.

On the title given to Christ the renderings differ by a shade. Ellicott traces the word through its other occurrences, where it means first a leader and then an originator, and settles on Author, though he will not let the notion of going first be lost in a passage that shows the Lord taking man's lot upon him. Robertson allows either, calling him a pioneer blazing the way, and also the Elder Brother of us all. Henry keeps the leading uppermost: those who are saved must come to salvation under a captain sufficient for the purpose. On the making perfect, Robertson removes the scruple at once, since it is the humanity in view and nothing is said of sin; Clarke states the bare necessity, that without suffering he could not die and without dying could not atone. Here Wesley enters a caution the others do not. What is said of the Lord's being perfected through sufferings has, he insists, no relation to our being sanctified by ours; he was perfect as God and as man before ever he suffered, and by suffering was made a complete sin-offering, which is as far out of our sphere as his ascension. Calvin had drawn the opposite comfort, that the faithful are sanctified for glory by sorrows as their head was, and may therefore kiss the cross rather than dread it.

The eleventh verse turns on two words. On the first, Clarke argues it does not merely mean to make holy but to make atonement, answering to the Hebrew term for expiation, and cites the saying that for their sakes I sanctify myself, that is, consecrate myself as a sacrifice. Barnes reports that three commentators he respects would render the clause the expiator and the expiated, allows the word may bear it, but doubts the sense is needed and prefers the fuller idea of consecration. Calvin lists the three senses the verb carries and chooses purification, noting that others prefer expiation as better suited to a passage about atonement. Ellicott finds the epistle's own usage to be a bringing into fellowship with God, and he and Robertson both mark the present participle, so that the sanctifying is a process and not a completed act. Gill traces it to its sources: they are sanctified in Christ, from him and by him, by his blood and by his Spirit. On the second word the field is wider still. Clarke says father, family, blood, seed, race and nature have all been proposed, and prefers nature; Calvin agrees, taking it as one mass, though several fathers and moderns read it of God; Ellicott and Robertson read it of one Father, which is what links the verse to the many sons before. All of them end where the verse does, that he is not ashamed to own them.
12:
The first citation comes from a psalm whose Messianic reference none disputes. Ellicott calls it remarkable for its closeness to the Passion narratives, and says that whether the inscription naming David stands or it was written after the Captivity, its reference is certain; he will not class it with those taken as directly prophetic, since some verses are too definite not to describe actual experience, and calls it typically prophetic. Gill argues from the title, the morning hind, and from the detail of the sufferings, ruling out the nation, Esther and David together. Barnes states the use made of it exactly: the weight lies not on declaring the name but on the word brethren. He notes it would have been easy to appeal to the Lord's familiar use of that word to his disciples, but that this would not serve with readers who had been Jews, for whom the point had to stand in their own Scriptures. On the second half of the verse three of them hear music. Robertson finds a picture of public worship with the Messiah sharing in it, Wesley makes him the precentor of the choir, doing this literally among his apostles the night before the passion, and Calvin says it is a powerful stimulant to know that Christ leads our songs and composes our hymns.

The next clause divides them evenly, and the question is where it comes from. Ellicott takes it from the same chapter of Isaiah that certainly supplies the words after it. Barnes agrees, on three grounds: the Greek matches the Septuagint exactly, the next verse is quoted immediately, and no other passage carries the same expression. He names the critics who agree, and observes that the psalm proposed instead was never reckoned Messianic even by the Jews. Robertson takes the same view without argument. Clarke is not so sure; the place is not clear to him, thinking it most probably a psalm of David, parts of which seem to belong to the Messiah. Calvin holds that reading and defends it. The whole psalm concerns one who was eminently a type of the Messiah, and its contents show David spoke in the person of another, since there appeared in him only a faint shadow of what is described: he boasts of being made head of the heathen, of unknown peoples yielding at the mere report of his name, whereas David subdued a few neighbouring nations by arms. Gill argues the same way, adding the Targum and the older Jewish application of the psalm.

The last citation carries the argument furthest. Ellicott shows the double position of the prophet, who delivers the divine message and then, in these words, retires to stand among the people, so that their attitude towards God's word must be his own; and he takes that as symbolising the double nature of the one whom every prophet typified. He recalls that in Isaiah the sons are joined to their father in the message, warning and promise carried in the symbolic names they bore. Clarke makes an observation about method that governs all three quotations: the fragments do not bear the argument by themselves, but are catch-words of whole paragraphs which, taken together, are full to the point. He proves it from this last one, since the sentence continues that the children are for signs and wonders in Israel, which Jesus and his disciples abundantly were, and which may take in all Christians throughout the earth. Robertson observes that the children here are the sons whom God was bringing to glory a few verses back, so the chain holds. Wesley draws the two clauses together: sharing his brethren's suffering as well as their nature he trusts God to carry him through, and then, owning them as younger brothers still in childhood, presents them all before God. Barnes puts it shortest: in such language the Messiah speaks as a man.
14:
Ellicott notes the Greek has blood and flesh, the familiar order reversed, the phrase naming human nature on its material side; Robertson confirms the reading and adds that the two verbs differ, the children having become partners in it while the Son took part of it. Who the children are divides Gill from Clarke. Gill confines them to the sons given to Christ, excluding the men of this world, Abraham's natural seed and mere professors; Clarke widens them to the whole race, explaining the narrower language as Jewish phraseology natural in a letter to Hebrews. On the purpose, Barnes states the logic plainly: an angel does not die, and the Son in his divine nature could not, so he took a form in which he could. Calvin says the same with more warmth: the overflowing of his love appears just here, that he put on our nature to make himself capable of dying. On the verb rendered destroy, all deny it means killing: Ellicott gives bring to nought, Barnes bringing into subjection, Robertson rendering idle, and Calvin the practical form, that though the devil still attempts our ruin his power to hurt us is restrained. Wesley puts the relation in an image, that death is the devil's servant and serjeant, handing over those he seizes in sin.

The fifteenth verse is felt by all, and they differ chiefly on who is meant. Ellicott supposes the words prompted by the writer's sympathy with persecuted readers, and says the crushing power of that fear over those who have not grasped that life and immortality are brought to light is beyond reckoning. Clarke thinks the Gentiles chiefly in view, having no certainty of immortality, and adds that those who know not God are in continual torment because they dread something beyond death; he supports it with a long quotation from Hamlet. Robertson observes that the ancients feared death greatly though their philosophers argued against it, and calls the phrase a picture of bond-slaves of fear. Calvin turns it back on the believer: nothing but a curse appears in death looked at apart from Christ, and a man who cannot quiet his mind about it has made little proficiency in faith, extreme fear being a certain evidence of unbelief. Barnes softens that by asking what a Christian has to fear on the dying bed, in the grave, or at the judgment, being everywhere under his Saviour's eye. Gill notes only a second end of the incarnation.

On the sixteenth verse the translators are corrected with one voice. Ellicott says the margin comes near the true meaning while the text confuses the argument: it is not of angels he takes hold, but of the seed of Abraham; Clarke agrees, and thinks it strange so many missed so obvious a sense. Both allow the verb cannot simply mean to help, but insist it suggests laying hold in order to help; Ellicott illustrates it from the Gospel healings and traces the language to the prophets, where God takes Israel by the hand from the ends of the earth. Barnes gives the range of the word, from seizing and detaining to taking a man by the hand to aid him, and takes the latter. Chrysostom supplies the picture the others only imply: the word comes from pursuing those who turn away, doing everything to overtake them as they flee, so that when our nature was fleeing far away he pursued and overtook us. Clarke draws it the same way: the rebel angels were let fall until they fell into perdition, while man, falling too, was caught. Henry says it plainly, that as their tree fell so it lies. Gill guards the negative: angels are not denied help but only the assuming of their nature, which could not die and so could not atone; and Calvin, that we were preferred not for our excellence but for our misery.
17:
The seventeenth verse states an obligation, and Robertson takes the verb strictly: it is the word for owing, so that having undertaken redemption voluntarily, the Son was bound to be properly equipped for a priestly service. Ellicott joins the phrase in all things to the being made like, and lists what the likeness had to include, liability to temptation, sorrow, pain and death, noting that the one exception is not in view; Robertson names it, the yielding to sin, and admits how hard it is to comprehend real temptation in the Son of God. Gill works through the likeness and keeps qualifying it: in all the essentials of the nature, though not by natural generation; in all properties and affections that are not sinful, but not in sin nor sickness; and in all temptations, though his differed, since none arose from within and those from without made no impression. Calvin puts it positively and warns against holding it coldly. Two things are to be considered in Christ's human nature, the real flesh and the feelings that belong to a man, and he took both; all knowledge of this without feeling our own need of the benefit is lifeless.

The two adjectives then divide the office between them. Robertson says they touch its chief points, sympathy toward men and fidelity toward God, and sharpens it by recalling that the high priests of that generation were political tools chosen by Rome. Ellicott finds the Greek order throwing weight on compassionate, which suits the tone of the chapter, and states the principle: one who has not so understood his brethren's infirmities as to be compassionate cannot be their faithful representative before God. He attaches faithful more closely to what follows, so that the fidelity is proved by the suffering of death. Wesley divides them in four words, merciful toward sinners and faithful toward God, and defines a priest as one having right of approach who brings others with him. Clarke takes the same double view: this priest secures God's honour on one side and makes and applies the atonement on the other. Calvin notices what the rest pass over, that the sentence is built as the prophets often build: compassionate, then faithful high priest, then the atonement, then the helping of the tempted, so that the first member answers the last and the second the third.

The last verse rests on a maxim Clarke states: a state of suffering disposes men to be compassionate, and those who endure most feel most for others. He proves it from a line of Virgil, that one not ignorant of evil learns to succour the wretched, and gives Dryden's rendering. Calvin, independently, reaches for the same line, remarking that the poet must have drawn it from daily examples, but then guards it: the Son of God needed no experience to know the emotions of mercy, yet we could not have been persuaded he is ready to help us had he not become acquainted by experience with our miseries. Barnes widens the word rendered tempted, which in Greek means to put to the proof, whether by affliction or by an inducement to evil, and says the Saviour met both in the severest form; a man who was never sick, or never buried a friend, is poorly qualified to comfort. Robertson makes the perfect tense permanent, so the suffering remains part of Christ's experience, traces the temptation to escape the cross from the wilderness through Peter to Gethsemane, and says the word able is the heart of it, the power to help resting on the humanity as well as the deity. Ellicott hesitates between two renderings of the opening words and allows that one seems to limit the help, though that vanishes against the infinitude of the life. Gill counts the outward slights and desertions among the temptations; Wesley, that the suffering was itself the demonstrative proof.
